script:
Roth or traditional 401(k)?
Stop guessing.
Start with one question:
Do you want to pay taxes now, or later?
Traditional contributions go in before taxes.
That lowers your taxable income today, but your contributions and earnings are taxed when you withdraw them.
Roth contributions go in after taxes.
You get no break today, but qualified withdrawals, including the growth, are tax-free.
Here's the math almost nobody shows you.
Say you're in the 24% tax bracket and have $10,000 of income to invest.
Traditional lets you invest all $10,000.
Roth means paying $2,400 in tax first, so $7,600 goes in.
Both options reduce your take-home pay by the same $7,600.
Now say the money quadruples.
Traditional grows to $40,000.
Roth grows to $30,400.
If your retirement tax rate is 22%, traditional leaves you $31,200 after tax.
That beats the tax-free Roth by $800.
But if your retirement rate is 32%, traditional leaves just $27,200.
Now Roth wins by $3,200.
And if your rate stays at 24%, both leave you $30,400.
So ask yourself three questions.
Am I in my peak earning years, or is my income temporarily low?
Do I expect my tax rate to be higher or lower in retirement?
Do I need the deduction now, or can I pay the tax today?
Higher rate now usually favors traditional.
Higher rate later usually favors Roth.
And if you're unsure, you can split contributions between both.
That's tax diversification.
Do your own research, especially if you're near retirement.
Which one are you using right now, Roth or traditional?
If you're looking to grow your net worth, follow me.

sources.supports: Traditional contributions are pre-tax and taxable with earnings at withdrawal; Roth contributions are taxed currently; qualified Roth withdrawals of contributions and earnings are tax-free.

Workers may contribute to both traditional pre-tax and designated Roth accounts in the same year, in any proportion; qualified Roth distributions require the five-year participation period and age 59½, death, or disability.
